concepts.title: 9–9.1 Discounting Techniques and the Net Present Value Method
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (May 2024 Q3(a), Jan 2025 Q3(a), Sep 2025 Q1(c)) · RTP 2 (May 2024, May 2025) · MTP 1 (May 2026 Series I)
understand: ==**Discounting techniques consider the time value of money and discount the cash flows to their present value.** They are also known as **Present Value techniques**: NPV, IRR, PI and the discounted payback period — with MIRR added in §9.5.==

==**The net present value of a project is the amount, in current value of amount, the investment earns after paying cost of capital in each period.**==
==**Net present value = Present value of net cash inflow − Total net initial investment**==
Since additional investment may be required during the project's life, the appropriate general formula is
==**Net present value = Present value of cash inflows − Present value of cash outflows**==
==**NPV = C₁/(1+k) + C₂/(1+k)² + C₃/(1+k)³ + … + Cₙ/(1+k)ⁿ − I**, where **C** = cash flow of various years, **k** = discount rate, **n** = life of the project and **I** = investment.==

==**The five steps** (SM §9.1): 1. Determine the net cash inflow in each year. 2. Select the desired rate of return, discounting rate or WACC. 3. Find the discount factor for each year based on that rate. 4. Multiply the cash flows by the respective discount factors to get the present value of each. 5. Total the present values.==

==**Decision rule.** If **NPV ≥ 0 — accept** the proposal. If **NPV < 0 — reject** it. ==The NPV method can be used to select between mutually exclusive projects: **the one with the higher NPV should be selected.**==

**SM Illustration 3, the minimal worked example.** Net investment ₹1,00,000; net cash flows ₹55,000, ₹80,000 and ₹15,000; cost of capital 10% with PVIF 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751. Discounted: ₹49,995 + ₹66,080 + ₹11,265 = ₹1,27,340; ==**NPV = ₹27,340 — positive, so accept.**==

**SM Illustration 4, four projects at 12%.** Initial investments ₹2,00,000 / ₹1,90,000 / ₹2,50,000 / ₹2,10,000 for projects A to D. ==NPVs: **A ₹(19,750) · B ₹25,635 · C ₹27,050 · D ₹(3,750)**== — so A and D are rejected outright, and between B and C the higher NPV, C, wins on the NPV rule. (The same four projects return in §11.1 under a capital spending limit of ₹5,00,000.)

==**Advantages of NPV** (SM §9.1): it **takes into account the time value of money**; **the whole stream of cash flows is considered**; the net present value **can be seen as the addition to the wealth of shareholders**, so the criterion **is in conformity with basic financial objectives**; and because it expresses cash flows in current rupees, **the NPVs of different projects can be compared** and each project evaluated independently on its own merit.==

==**Limitations of NPV** (SM §9.1): it **involves difficult calculations**; it **necessitates forecasting cash flows and the discount rate**, so its accuracy depends on the accuracy of two estimates that are hard to make in practice; and ==**the decision is based on an absolute measure — it ignores the difference in initial outflows and the size of different proposals when evaluating mutually exclusive projects.**==

That last limitation is the whole reason §9.2 exists. **NPV tells you how much wealth a project adds; it does not tell you how much wealth it adds per rupee committed** — and when capital is limited, that second question is the one that matters.
concepts.example: September 2025's Global Beverage Corporation is the past paper every candidate should work, because its NPV comes out **negative** — ₹(2,63,870) — and the mark is in saying so. A chapter learned only from positive-NPV illustrations produces candidates who compute correctly and then recommend acceptance out of habit.

provisions.exam_angle: Use the PV-of-outflows form whenever an outflow falls after year 0 — additional working capital, a mid-life overhaul, a replacement part.

provisions.exam_angle: Note the rule is 'greater than or equal to zero' — a nil NPV is accepted, because the project exactly earns its cost of capital.

provisions.requirement: NPV ignores the difference in initial outflows and the size of proposals when comparing mutually exclusive projects.
provisions.exam_angle: This limitation is what PI, and capital rationing in §11.1, are there to answer.

memory.trick: **NPV is wealth in today's rupees.** Positive means the project pays for its capital and leaves something over; nil means it exactly pays for its capital, which is still acceptable; negative means it does not.

mistakes: Discounting the year-0 outflow by a factor; the factor for year 0 is 1.000.
Stopping at the number without the decision; 'NPV is positive, therefore accept' is part of the answer.
Recommending acceptance where the NPV is negative, because every illustration in the book was positive.
Treating a nil NPV as a rejection; the rule is NPV ≥ 0.
Comparing the NPVs of projects with different initial outlays as though NPV answered that question — it does not, which is the point of PI.

official_questions.question: HCP Ltd., a manufacturer of railway parts, is considering replacing machine A with a new CNC machine B. Machine A has a book value of ₹4,80,000 and a remaining economic life of 6 years; it could be sold now for ₹1,80,000 and has zero salvage value at the end of year 6. Machine B costs ₹24,00,000 with a 6-year life, plus ₹1,40,000 for installation and ₹60,000 for testing; a government subsidy of 15% of the purchase price will be received at the end of year 1; salvage value at the end of year 6 will be ₹3,20,000. Annual savings: three skilled workers at ₹1,68,000 each, ₹4,80,000 of reduced wastage and defectives, and ₹3,50,000 of sales no longer lost to delays. New costs: a trained technician at ₹3,90,000 and ₹1,54,000 more of operation and maintenance. Tax 30%; required return 14%; straight line depreciation; ignore tax savings on the loss on sale of the existing machine. Required: (i) NPV and profitability index, with advice; (ii) the discounted pay-back period.
answer_points: ==**Net initial cash outflow.** Cost of new machine ₹24,00,000 **less** sale proceeds of the existing machine ₹1,80,000 **add** installation ₹1,40,000 **add** testing ₹60,000 **less** the subsidy — and the subsidy is **received at the end of year 1, so it enters at its present value**: 15% × ₹24,00,000 = ₹3,60,000 × 0.877 = ₹3,15,720. **Net initial cash outflow = ₹21,04,280.**==

==**Incremental depreciation.** Depreciation on the existing machine = ₹4,80,000 ÷ 6 = ₹80,000. The new machine's **depreciation base** is ₹24,00,000 + ₹1,40,000 + ₹60,000 **less the subsidy ₹3,60,000** (at face value, not discounted) **less salvage ₹3,20,000** = **₹19,20,000**, so depreciation = ₹19,20,000 ÷ 6 = ₹3,20,000. **Incremental depreciation = ₹3,20,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹2,40,000.**==

**Annual operating CFAT.** Savings: 3 × ₹1,68,000 = ₹5,04,000 + ₹4,80,000 + ₹3,50,000 = **₹13,34,000**. Less increased costs ₹3,90,000 + ₹1,54,000 = ₹5,44,000. **Incremental saving before tax and depreciation ₹7,90,000**; less incremental depreciation ₹2,40,000 = **incremental PBT ₹5,50,000**; less tax at 30% ₹1,65,000 = **PAT ₹3,85,000**; add depreciation ₹2,40,000 = ==**incremental CFAT ₹6,25,000 a year**==.
==**Profitability index** = ₹25,75,920 ÷ ₹21,04,280 = **1.224**. Since the NPV is positive and the PI greater than 1, **the company should replace the machine.**==

**(ii) Discounted payback period.** Discounted CFAT: ₹5,48,125, ₹4,80,625, ₹4,21,875, ₹3,70,000, ₹3,24,375 and ₹4,30,920 (year 6 carrying the salvage), with cumulative present values ₹5,48,125, ₹10,28,750, ₹14,50,625, ₹18,20,625, ₹21,45,000 and ₹25,75,920. The outlay of ₹21,04,280 is passed during year 5, so ==**discounted payback = 4 + (₹21,04,280 − ₹18,20,625) ÷ ₹3,24,375 = 4 + 0.874 = 4.87 years**==.

==**The two subsidy traps, which are the question's real content.** The subsidy is received at the **end of year 1**, so it is discounted when it reduces the outflow — but it reduces the **depreciation base at face value**, because depreciation is computed on cost net of grant, not on a present value. Candidates who discount it in both places, or in neither, lose both marks.==

**And one instruction to obey literally.** 'Ignore tax savings on loss due to sale of existing machine' removes what would otherwise be a tax benefit on the ₹3,00,000 book loss (₹4,80,000 − ₹1,80,000). Do not supply it.
official_questions.conclusion: NPV ₹4,71,640, PI 1.224, discounted payback 4.87 years — replace. The subsidy is discounted in the outflow and undiscounted in the depreciation base.
keywords: subsidy at the end of year 1
depreciation base net of subsidy and salvage

official_questions.question: SRT Limited, a steel rod manufacturer, is considering an aluminium smelting and moulding plant costing ₹20,00,000 to purchase and install, with a 5-year useful life and residual value ₹1,00,000. Production and sales 1,00,000 units a year; selling price ₹150; direct cost ₹100; fixed cost including depreciation ₹8,00,000 a year. Marketing and promotion costs not included above are ₹1,00,000 in year 1 and ₹1,60,000 in year 2. Investment in debtors and stocks will rise in year 1 by ₹1,50,000 and ₹2,00,000; creditors will rise by ₹1,00,000 in year 1; debtors, stocks and creditors are recouped at the end of year 5. Cost of capital 18%; tax 30% paid in the year profits are made; depreciation tax deductible, straight line. PV factors at 18%: 0.847, 0.718, 0.609, 0.516, 0.437. Required: (i) NPV and profitability index; (ii) advise whether the plant should be purchased.
answer_points: ==**Two figures have to be extracted before the table can be built.** **Depreciation** = (₹20,00,000 − ₹1,00,000) ÷ 5 = **₹3,80,000**. Since fixed cost of ₹8,00,000 **includes** depreciation, the **fixed cash cost is ₹8,00,000 − ₹3,80,000 = ₹4,20,000**. Using ₹8,00,000 as a cash cost and then also deducting depreciation double counts it.==
==**Net working capital** = debtors ₹1,50,000 + stocks ₹2,00,000 − creditors ₹1,00,000 = **₹2,50,000**.==
**Year 5 carries two extras**: working capital released ₹2,50,000 and residual value ₹1,00,000, so its net inflow is **₹36,70,000**.
==**Profitability index** = ₹1,03,94,884 ÷ ₹22,50,000 = **4.62**. Since the NPV is positive and the PI greater than 1, **the plant should be purchased.**==

**ICAI's own alternative.** If the working capital is assumed to be introduced at the **end** of year 1 instead, the outflow becomes ₹20,00,000 + (₹2,50,000 × 0.847) = ₹22,11,750, and the NPV rises to ₹81,83,134 with a PI of 1,03,94,884 ÷ 22,11,750 = 4.70. **State the assumption you are using** — ICAI accepts either, but not a silent mix.

**Why the PI is so large.** A ₹22.50 lakh outlay generating ₹33 lakh a year is extraordinary by the standards of an exam question. That is a reminder that **a PI is only as meaningful as the outflow in its denominator**: here the plant is cheap relative to the trade it supports.
official_questions.conclusion: NPV ₹81,44,884 and PI 4.62 — purchase. Net working capital is ₹2,50,000, and the fixed cash cost is ₹4,20,000, not ₹8,00,000.
keywords: recouped at the end of year 5

official_questions.question: Global Beverage Corporation is considering replacing a bottling machine with a newer, more efficient model. The existing machine was bought five years ago for ₹16,00,000 and has a total useful life of ten years; it can be sold now for ₹9,60,000. The new machine costs ₹32,00,000, with an estimated salvage value of ₹3,20,000 and a useful life of five years. With the new machine the annual contribution margin rises from ₹16,00,000 to ₹18,40,000 and operating efficiencies yield further annual savings of ₹3,20,000. Depreciation straight line over five years. Cost of capital 12%; tax 33%. Calculate the NPV of the new machine. PVIFA(12%, 5) = 3.605; PVIF(12%, 5) = 0.567.
answer_points: **Savings.** Incremental contribution ₹18,40,000 − ₹16,00,000 = **₹2,40,000**; add the operating cost saving ₹3,20,000; **total savings ₹5,60,000 a year**.

==**Incremental depreciation.** New machine: (₹32,00,000 − ₹3,20,000) ÷ 5 = **₹5,76,000**. Old machine: ₹16,00,000 ÷ 10 = **₹1,60,000** — and that charge **continues for the five years the old machine would have had left**, so it is the depreciation given up. **Incremental depreciation = ₹5,76,000 − ₹1,60,000 = ₹4,16,000.**==

**CFAT.** Savings ₹5,60,000 less incremental depreciation ₹4,16,000 = **incremental PBT ₹1,44,000**; less tax at 33% ₹47,520 = **PAT ₹96,480**; add depreciation back ₹4,16,000 = ==**cash inflow ₹5,12,480 a year**==.
**Present value of the inflows.** ₹5,12,480 × 3.605 = ₹18,47,490, plus the salvage value ₹3,20,000 × 0.567 = ₹1,81,440, giving **₹20,28,930**.

==**Initial outflow.** Cost of the new machine ₹32,00,000 less sale proceeds of the existing machine ₹9,60,000 = ₹22,40,000, **plus the tax on the gain on that sale**: the old machine's book value after five years is ₹16,00,000 − (5 × ₹1,60,000) = ₹8,00,000, so the gain is ₹1,60,000 and the tax at 33% is ₹52,800. **Net initial outflow = ₹22,92,800.**==
==**NPV = ₹20,28,930 − ₹22,92,800 = ₹(2,63,870) — negative, so the machine should not be replaced.**==

**ICAI's alternative.** If the tax on the sale of the existing machine is **not** taken, the outflow is ₹22,40,000 and the NPV is ₹(2,11,070) — still negative, so the decision does not change. ICAI prints both.

==**The lesson of this question is the conclusion, not the arithmetic.** It is the only replacement question in the official set that comes out negative. The savings of ₹5,60,000 a year look generous against a ₹22.40 lakh net outlay, but five years at 12% is a PVAF of only 3.605 — and once tax takes a third of the pre-depreciation benefit, the inflows do not reach the outlay. **Compute, then read the sign, then answer the question that was asked.**==
official_questions.conclusion: NPV ₹(2,63,870) — do not replace. Both of ICAI's treatments of the tax on the old machine's sale leave the NPV negative.
keywords: tax on sale of existing machine

official_questions.question: HMR Ltd. is considering replacing a manually operated old machine with a fully automatic new machine. The old machine is fully depreciated for tax purposes but has a book value of ₹2,50,000; it cannot fetch more than ₹40,000 if sold now and will have no realisable value after 10 years. A trade-in allowance of ₹1,50,000 has been offered on the new machine, which is priced at ₹6,00,000 before the allowance. The new machine's expected life is 10 years with a salvage value of ₹35,000. The company follows written down value depreciation at 10% in its books but straight line depreciation for tax purposes, this being the only machine in the block of assets. Working capital of ₹50,000 is needed, released at the end of year 10. Old machine: output 60,000 units, selling price ₹18, operating hours 2,800, material ₹5 a unit, labour ₹50 an hour, indirect cash cost ₹1,00,000 a year. New machine: output 80,000 units, selling price ₹18, operating hours 2,800, material ₹5 a unit, labour ₹75 an hour, indirect cash cost ₹1,75,000 a year. Opportunity cost of capital 10%; tax 30%; book profit treated as ordinary income. Analyse whether to replace, and estimate the IRR of the replacement decision. (ICAI label: Investment Decisions.)
answer_points: ==**The trade-in allowance, not the market price, is the figure that reduces the outflow.** The machine is priced at ₹6,00,000 'before allowance for trade in' and ₹1,50,000 is offered, so the **net cash price is ₹4,50,000**. The ₹40,000 open-market value is a distractor — the company is not selling on the market, it is trading in.==

==**But the trade-in creates a taxable book profit.** Book value ₹2,50,000 against a trade-in value of ₹1,50,000 gives a **book loss of ₹1,00,000**, and since book profit is treated as ordinary income, the loss gives a **tax saving of ₹30,000** at 30%. State the direction carefully: here it reduces the outflow.==
**Initial outflow** = net price ₹4,50,000 + working capital ₹50,000 − tax saving on the book loss ₹30,000.

**Incremental operating flows, built per unit and per hour.** Old machine: sales 60,000 × ₹18 = ₹10,80,000; material 60,000 × ₹5 = ₹3,00,000; labour 2,800 × ₹50 = ₹1,40,000; indirect cash cost ₹1,00,000. New machine: sales 80,000 × ₹18 = ₹14,40,000; material 80,000 × ₹5 = ₹4,00,000; labour 2,800 × ₹75 = ₹2,10,000; indirect cash cost ₹1,75,000. ==**Note that the operating hours are the same, so the labour cost rises only because of the higher rate — the automatic machine produces a third more output in the same hours.**==

==**Two depreciation rates, and only one of them matters.** The books use 10% WDV; **tax uses straight line**. Cash flow follows the **tax** depreciation, because that is what determines the tax paid. The book figure is there to be ignored, and ICAI's own illustration of the same question in SM §11.2 (Illustration 18) reverses the two methods to make the same point.==

**Terminal year** carries the salvage value ₹35,000, the release of working capital ₹50,000, and — since this is **the only machine in the block** — the short-term capital gain or loss on the sale under §6.1 Case 1.
**IRR.** With a level incremental inflow, start from PVAF = outflow ÷ annual inflow, locate the bracketing rates in the 10-year row, and interpolate (SM §9.3, Scenario 1).

==**A cross-reference worth making.** The study material's own **Illustration 18 is this same HMR Ltd. question** with different figures — book value ₹2,40,000, trade-in ₹1,00,000, price ₹4,50,000, tax depreciation at 7.5% WDV. Work both and the pattern becomes automatic.==
official_questions.conclusion: Trade-in allowance sets the outflow; the book loss gives a tax saving; cash flow follows the tax depreciation, not the book depreciation.
keywords: book profit treated as ordinary income

official_questions.question: Linty, a labour-oriented manufacturer in Chattisgarh, is considering an automatic machine to replace manual operations, choosing between models TMT 1 and TMT 2, each with a 10-year economic life. Cost of machine ₹45,00,000 and ₹50,00,000; estimated saving in direct wages ₹15,00,000 and ₹20,00,000 a year; saving in scrap ₹5,00,000 and ₹6,00,000; additional indirect material ₹2,00,000 each; additional indirect labour ₹1,50,000 and ₹1,80,000; additional repairs and maintenance ₹4,00,000 and ₹8,00,000. Straight line depreciation; tax 35%; expected rate of return 15%. The five MCQs ask for the annual saving from each machine, the payback period, the ARR and the profitability index. (ICAI label: Investment Decision.)
answer_points: **Depreciation.** No salvage value is given, so depreciation is cost ÷ 10: **₹4,50,000** for TMT 1 and **₹5,00,000** for TMT 2.

**Annual cash savings.** Total savings (wages + scrap) ₹20,00,000 and ₹26,00,000; total additional cash costs (indirect material + indirect labour + repairs) ₹7,50,000 and ₹11,80,000; ==**annual cash savings ₹12,50,000 and ₹14,20,000**==.
**Annual savings after tax.** Less depreciation gives ₹8,00,000 and ₹9,20,000 before tax; less tax at 35% gives ==**₹5,20,000 and ₹5,98,000**== — the answers to MCQs (i) and (ii).
**Annual cash inflows** = after-tax savings + depreciation = ==**₹9,70,000 and ₹10,98,000**==.
**Payback period** = cost ÷ annual cash inflow = ₹45,00,000 ÷ ₹9,70,000 = **4.63 years** and ₹50,00,000 ÷ ₹10,98,000 = **4.55 years**.

==**ARR on average investment** = after-tax saving ÷ average investment. With **no salvage value the average investment is simply half the cost** — ₹22,50,000 and ₹25,00,000 — so ARR = ₹5,20,000 ÷ ₹22,50,000 = **23.11%** and ₹5,98,000 ÷ ₹25,00,000 = **23.92%**.==

==**Every measure points the same way here — TMT 2 wins on payback, on ARR and on PI.** That unanimity is unusual, and it is worth noticing, because §9.7 is entirely about the cases where the measures disagree. When they all agree, the decision needs no further analysis.==
official_questions.conclusion: TMT 2 on every measure: payback 4.55 years against 4.63, ARR 23.92% against 23.11%, PI 1.10 against 1.08.
keywords: average investment is half the cost

official_questions.question: A company wants to invest in machinery costing ₹50,000 at the beginning of year 1. Net cash inflows from operations will be ₹18,000 a year for 3 years if the company services part of the machine at the end of year 1 at ₹10,000, in which case the scrap value at the end of year 3 will be ₹12,500. If it decides not to service the part, the part must be replaced at the end of year 2 at ₹15,400, but the machine will then work for a fourth year as well with an operational inflow of ₹18,000, and be scrapped at the end of year 4 for ₹9,000. Cost of capital 10%; ignore taxes. Recommend on NPV, and state the decision if the supplier gives a ₹5,000 discount on purchase.
answer_points:
==**Option II — replace the part at the end of year 2, four-year life.**
NPV = −₹50,000 + ₹18,000 × 2.4868 − (₹15,400 × 0.8264) + (₹27,000 × 0.6830)
= −₹50,000 + ₹44,762 − ₹12,727 + ₹18,441 = ==**+₹476 — positive.**==
**Note the ₹27,000 in year 4**: the fourth year's operational inflow of ₹18,000 **plus** the scrap of ₹9,000.
==**With the ₹5,000 discount.** The discount reduces the year-0 outflow in full, so it adds ₹5,000 to each NPV: Option I becomes **+₹62** and Option II becomes **+₹5,476**.==

**ICAI's own wording on the conclusion is worth copying.** On Option I with the discount: 'Net Present Value is positive but very small; therefore, this option may not be advisable.' On Option II without the discount: 'Net Present Value is positive, but very low as compared to the investment.' ==A technically positive NPV of ₹476 on a ₹50,000 investment is not a recommendation — and saying so is what distinguishes a complete answer.==

**Why the two options have the same annuity.** Both earn ₹18,000 for three years, and ICAI uses PVAF(10%, 3) = 2.4868 for both. The whole difference between them is **when the repair falls and whether a fourth year exists** — which is why this is really a question about the timing of outflows, not about the size of inflows.

**One structural point.** The two options have **different lives** — three years and four — so strictly §11.2 applies and an equivalent annualised comparison would be the cleaner test. ICAI compares the raw NPVs here, which is defensible because the same machine is being bought either way and the question asks only whether to purchase.
official_questions.conclusion: Option I ₹(4,938); Option II +₹476; with the ₹5,000 discount, +₹62 and +₹5,476. Only Option II with the discount is a comfortable accept.
keywords: scrap added to the final year's inflow

official_questions.question: Mr. Anand is thinking of buying a share at ₹500 whose face value per share is ₹100. He is expecting a bonus at the ratio 1 : 5 at the end of the fourth year. The annual expected dividend is 20% and the same rate is expected to be maintained on the expanded capital base. He intends to sell the shares at the end of the seventh year at an expected price of ₹900 each. Incidental expenses for purchase and sale of shares are estimated to be 5% of the market price. Assuming a discount rate of 12% per annum, COMPUTE the net present value from the acquisition of the shares.
answer_points: ==**The two things the 1 : 5 bonus changes, and the point of the whole question.** From the end of year 4, Mr. Anand holds **1.2 shares** — one bought share plus one-fifth of a bonus share. So from **year 5 onwards** both the dividend and the eventual sale proceeds are computed on 1.2 shares, not on 1.==

==**Dividend per share.** 20% on the **face value of ₹100** = **₹20 per share per year**, not 20% of the ₹500 purchase price. On the expanded base from year 5 the annual dividend becomes ₹100 × 1.2 × 20% = **₹24**.==
==**Year 7 — net sale proceeds.** ₹900 × 1.2 = ₹1,080, less incidental expenses of 5% = **₹1,026**; × 0.452 = **463.75**.==
==**Initial outflow at year 0.** Purchase price ₹500 **plus** incidental expenses of 5% = **₹525**, taken at a discount factor of 1.==

**Where the value actually comes from.** Of the ₹561.14 of inflows, ₹463.75 — **83%** — is the terminal sale. Seven years of dividends contribute ₹97.39. The investment is a bet on the exit price, and the NPV of ₹36.14 on an outlay of ₹525 is a margin of under 7%: a small fall in the expected ₹900 would wipe it out.

**Note on the incidental expenses.** They work in opposite directions and both must be applied: on purchase they **increase** the outflow (₹500 → ₹525); on sale they **reduce** the inflow (₹1,080 → ₹1,026). Applying them once, or in the same direction twice, is the commonest arithmetic slip in this question.
official_questions.conclusion: The net present value from the acquisition is ₹36.14, so the purchase is worthwhile at a discount rate of 12% — but 83% of the value rests on the terminal sale price of ₹900, which leaves a thin margin of safety.
official_questions.marks_split: 1 mark for the 1.2-share position from year 4, 1 mark for the dividend on face value and its increase from year 5, 1 mark for the net sale proceeds, 1 mark for the grossed-up initial outflow, 1 mark for the NPV.
official_questions.mistake: Computing the dividend as 20% of the ₹500 market price (₹100 a year) rather than 20% of the ₹100 face value (₹20 a year). The second is applying the bonus from year 4's dividend rather than from year 5 — the bonus arrives **at the end** of year 4, so year 4's dividend is still on one share.

official_questions.question: Vyom Limited, an IT conglomerate, is planning to take over Aryayash Limited, a startup incorporated two years ago but holding a lot of prospects. To determine the buyout consideration, Vyom Limited has asked you to estimate the fair value of the startup today based on future earnings estimates. Expected sales in the coming year are ₹25 lakh with a P/V ratio of 40%. Sales are expected to grow at 20% for the next two years, at 40% for a further two years and at 25% in the sixth year, and thereafter cash flows grow at a constant 10%. Fixed costs are ₹12 lakh for the first two years and ₹10 lakh thereafter. Tax is 25% and Vyom Limited's desired rate of return is 15%.
answer_points: ==**The principle, stated first.** Fair value of a company = the **present value of all its future cash flows discounted at the expected rate of return of the acquiring company**. The discount rate is **Vyom Limited's** 15%, not the startup's — ICAI prints that as a note because it is the step candidates get wrong.==

==**Contribution at 40% of sales, year by year (₹ lakh).** Year 1: 10.00 on sales of 25. Year 2: 12.00 (sales 30, +20%). Year 3: 14.40 (sales 36, +20%). Year 4: 20.16 (sales 50.4, +40%). Year 5: 28.22 (sales 70.56, +40%). Year 6: 35.28 (sales 88.20, +25%).==
==**Less fixed cost** (12 for years 1 and 2, 10 thereafter) gives **NPBT**: −2.00, 0.00, 4.40, 10.16, 18.22, 25.28.==

==**The loss set-off, which is the second thing candidates miss.** Year 1's loss of ₹2 lakh is carried forward and set off in **year 3**, so year 3's taxable income is 4.40 − 2.00 = **2.40**, not 4.40. Years 2 and 4 to 6 need no adjustment.==

==**Tax at 25% and cash flow (NPBT less tax).** Year 1 tax nil, cash flow **−2.00**. Year 2 nil, **0.00**. Year 3 tax 0.60, **3.80**. Year 4 tax 2.54, **7.62**. Year 5 tax 4.55, **13.66**. Year 6 tax 6.32, **18.96**.==
==**Discount years 1 to 6 at 15%:** −1.740, 0, 2.50, 4.35, 6.79, 8.19 — a total present value of **₹20.08 lakh**.==

==**The terminal value, which is where almost all the value sits.** From year 7 the cash flow grows at a constant 10%, so the value at the end of year 6 = 18.96 × 1.10 ÷ (0.15 − 0.10) = **₹417.12 lakh**. Discounted back at the 15% six-year factor of 0.432: **₹180.20 lakh**.==
==**Total fair value of Aryayash Limited** = 20.08 + 180.20 = **₹200.28 lakh**.==

**What the structure of the answer tells Vyom Limited's board.** ₹180.20 lakh of the ₹200.28 lakh — **90%** — is the terminal value, which rests entirely on the assumption that cash flows grow at 10% for ever from year 7. The six years that have actually been forecast are worth only ₹20.08 lakh. A valuation with that shape should be stress-tested on the terminal growth rate before any price is offered: at 8% perpetual growth the terminal value falls to ₹297.94 lakh and the fair value to about ₹149 lakh.

**ICAI's second note, worth one line.** The terminal value is the value at the point **from which** cash flows grow at a constant rate, and it is assumed that from year 7 the **cash flow or NPAT** grows at the constant rate — not sales. Growing sales at 10% and recomputing contribution and tax would give a different and wrong figure.
official_questions.conclusion: The fair value of Aryayash Limited today is ₹200.28 lakh — ₹20.08 lakh from the six forecast years and ₹180.20 lakh from the terminal value of ₹417.12 lakh discounted at Vyom Limited's own required return of 15%. Ninety per cent of the value is terminal, so the price Vyom offers should be tested against a lower perpetual growth assumption.
official_questions.marks_split: 1 mark for the contribution schedule, 1 mark for the loss set-off in year 3, 1 mark for the discounted cash flows of years 1 to 6, 1½ marks for the terminal value and its discounting, ½ mark for using the acquirer's discount rate.
official_questions.mistake: Discounting at a rate built for the startup rather than Vyom Limited's desired 15%. The second is forgetting the carry-forward of year 1's loss into year 3, which overstates year 3's tax by ₹50,000 and the fair value with it. The third is growing **sales** at 10% beyond year 6 instead of growing the **cash flow**.

mcqs.question: A project needs a net investment of ₹1,00,000 and generates net cash flows of ₹55,000, ₹80,000 and ₹15,000 over three years. At a cost of capital of 10% (PVIF 0.909, 0.826, 0.751) its NPV is:
mcqs.explanation: SM Illustration 3: the discounted inflows are ₹49,995, ₹66,080 and ₹11,265, totalling ₹1,27,340, from which the investment of ₹1,00,000 is deducted to give an NPV of ₹27,340. Since it is positive the project should be accepted.

why_wrong.B: The undiscounted total inflow less the investment — the time value of money has not been applied.
why_wrong.C: That is the present value of the inflows, before deducting the investment.
why_wrong.D: The sign is wrong; the discounted inflows exceed the investment.

mcqs.trap: Option C is the number most of the arithmetic produces; the last subtraction is what makes it an NPV.

mcqs.question: The study material describes the NPV decision as 'based on an absolute measure'. The consequence it draws from this is that NPV:

options.A: Cannot be used for mutually exclusive projects at all
options.B: Ignores the difference in initial outflows and the size of different proposals when evaluating mutually exclusive projects
options.C: Cannot be compared across projects because it is expressed in rupees
options.D: Assumes that cash flows are reinvested at the internal rate of return

mcqs.explanation: SM §9.1, limitations of NPV: the decision under the NPV method is based on an absolute measure, and it ignores the difference in initial outflows and the size of different proposals while evaluating mutually exclusive projects.

why_wrong.A: ICAI expressly says NPV can be used to select between mutually exclusive projects — the one with the higher NPV is selected.
why_wrong.C: The opposite: ICAI lists comparability in current rupees as an advantage of NPV.
why_wrong.D: That is the reinvestment assumption of IRR (§9.3.3); NPV assumes reinvestment at the discount rate.

mcqs.trap: Options C and D are both true statements about capital budgeting — but one is an advantage of NPV and the other belongs to IRR.

recap: NPV = PV of cash inflows − PV of cash outflows; accept if NPV ≥ 0; among mutually exclusive projects take the highest positive NPV.
Advantages: time value, whole stream of flows, addition to shareholder wealth, comparability.
Limitations: difficult calculation, dependence on two forecasts, and blindness to scale.
In a replacement question the figures are always incremental — incremental contribution, incremental depreciation, incremental cost.

concepts.title: 9.2 Profitability Index / Desirability Factor / Present Value Index Method
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 (asked with NPV in May 2024, Jan 2025, May 2025, May 2026) · RTP 1 (Jan 2026) · MTP 0
understand: ==Where a number of proposals have to be compared, each involving **different amounts of cash inflows**, one method is to work out the ==**'Desirability factor', or 'Profitability Index', or 'Present Value Index Method'**== — three names for the same ratio.

==**Profitability Index (PI) = Sum of discounted cash inflows ÷ Initial cash outlay, or total discounted cash outflow as the case may be.**==
The second denominator matters: **where outflows fall after year 0**, the denominator is their total present value, not just the year-0 figure.
==**Decision rule.** If **PI ≥ 1 — accept** the proposal. If **PI < 1 — reject** it. ==**In case of mutually exclusive projects, the project with the higher PI should be selected.**==

**SM Illustration 5.** Three projects with discounted cash outflows of ₹5,50,000, ₹75,000 and ₹1,00,20,000 and discounted inflows of ₹6,50,000, ₹95,000 and ₹1,00,30,000. Desirability factors: ==**1.18, 1.27 and 1.001**==. ==ICAI's own comment: **in absolute terms project 3 gives the highest cash inflows yet its desirability factor is low, because the outflow is also very high.** The desirability factor helps us in ranking various projects.==

==**Since PI is an extension of NPV, it has the same advantages and limitations.** Its own advantages (SM §9.2): it **uses the concept of time value of money**; and because the present value of inflows is **divided by** the present value of outflows, ==**it is a relative measure of a project's profitability**== — which is exactly what NPV is not.

==**Limitations of PI** (SM §9.2): it **fails as a guide in resolving capital rationing where projects are indivisible**; **once a single large project with high NPV is selected, the possibility of accepting several small projects which together may have a higher NPV is excluded**; and situations may arise where **a project with a lower profitability index generates cash flows in such a way that another project can be taken up one or two years later**, the total NPV then being more than that of the project with the highest PI. ==ICAI's conclusion: **the Profitability Index approach cannot be used indiscriminately** and all other types of project alternatives have to be worked out.==

**The relationship with NPV, which is what MCQs test.** ==**NPV = PV − I and PI = PV ÷ I**, so **PI = 1 + (NPV ÷ I)**.== A positive NPV therefore always means a PI above 1, and the two criteria **always agree on accept-or-reject**. They can disagree on **ranking**, and they do so whenever the outlays differ — which is the substance of RTP January 2026's question.
concepts.example: RTP January 2026 gives three projects with NPVs of ₹15, ₹20 and ₹25 thousand on investments of ₹60, ₹100 and ₹150 thousand. Project C has the highest NPV; Project A has the highest PI (1.25 against 1.20 and 1.167). Same three projects, two different winners — which is the examinable point.

official_questions.question: Consider the following data — Project A: NPV ₹15 thousand, investment ₹60 thousand; Project B: NPV ₹20 thousand, investment ₹100 thousand; Project C: NPV ₹25 thousand, investment ₹150 thousand. Given that NPV = PV − I and PI = PV ÷ I, which one of the following statements is correct? (A) Project A is recommended based on PI criterion (B) Project B is recommended based on NPV criterion (C) Project C is recommended based on PI criterion (D) Project A is recommended based on NPV criterion
answer_points: ==**Recover the present value of inflows first**, using the identity the question itself supplies: **PV = NPV + I**. Project A: ₹15 + ₹60 = **₹75**. Project B: ₹20 + ₹100 = **₹120**. Project C: ₹25 + ₹150 = **₹175** (all ₹'000).==

==**On the PI criterion the winner is Project A** (1.25, the highest). **On the NPV criterion the winner is Project C** (₹25 thousand, the highest). So **option (A) is correct** — Project A is recommended on the PI criterion.==
**Why each wrong option is wrong.** (B) Project B is best on neither criterion — it is second on both. (C) Project C has the **lowest** PI, not the highest. (D) Project A has the **lowest** NPV.

==**The structural point.** The project with the largest NPV has the smallest PI here, and that is not a coincidence: **PI = 1 + NPV ÷ I**, so a project can only have a high PI by having a small denominator. The rankings invert because the investments rise faster than the NPVs — ₹60 → ₹100 → ₹150 against ₹15 → ₹20 → ₹25.==

**Which criterion should actually be followed?** With no capital constraint, **NPV** — because it measures the addition to shareholders' wealth, and Project C adds the most. PI becomes the right criterion when capital is rationed and the projects are divisible, which is §11.1's 'NPV per rupee of capital' rule. ==The question asks only which criterion recommends which project, not which criterion is better.==
official_questions.conclusion: Option (A). PI picks A at 1.25; NPV picks C at ₹25 thousand — the same three projects, ranked in opposite order.

official_questions.question: Do the profitability index and the NPV criterion of evaluating investment proposals lead to the same acceptance-rejection and ranking decisions? In what SITUATIONS will they give conflicting results?
answer_points: ==**On acceptance and rejection — yes, always.** The two are linked by the identity **PI = 1 + NPV ÷ I**. So NPV ≥ 0 if and only if PI ≥ 1, and a project accepted on one criterion is accepted on the other. There is no set of cash flows on which they disagree about accept or reject.==

==**On ranking — no, not always.** NPV measures the **absolute** addition to wealth in rupees; PI measures the **relative** return per rupee invested. A project can be first on one and last on the other, and that is not an anomaly but the consequence of measuring two different things.==

==**The situation in which they conflict: mutually exclusive projects of different size.** Where the initial outlays differ, a large project may have the higher NPV while a small one has the higher PI, because the large project's bigger denominator holds its ratio down. ICAI's own illustration is the clearest form of it — Project A with an NPV of ₹15 thousand on ₹60 thousand (PI 1.25) against Project C with an NPV of ₹25 thousand on ₹150 thousand (PI 1.167): A wins on PI, C wins on NPV.==

**The second situation: capital rationing.** Where the capital available is limited, the question stops being 'which project adds most?' and becomes 'which combination adds most within the budget?'. PI, being NPV per rupee of capital, answers the second question and NPV does not — which is why §11.1 uses the PI ranking under rationing.

==**Which one to follow when they conflict.** **With no capital constraint, follow NPV**, because it measures the addition to the shareholders' wealth and that is the firm's objective; a higher ratio on a smaller base leaves money on the table. **Under capital rationing with divisible projects, follow PI**, because the constraint makes the return per rupee the binding consideration.==

**The limitation to record.** ICAI states that the profitability index **fails as a guide in resolving capital rationing where projects are indivisible**: once a single large project with a high NPV is selected, the possibility of accepting several small projects which together have a higher NPV is excluded. So PI's own home ground has a boundary.
official_questions.conclusion: They always agree on acceptance and rejection, because PI = 1 + NPV ÷ I. They can disagree on ranking whenever mutually exclusive projects differ in size, and the disagreement is resolved in favour of NPV where capital is unconstrained and in favour of PI where capital is rationed and the projects are divisible.
official_questions.marks_split: 1 mark for the identity and the accept-reject agreement, 2 marks for the ranking conflict with an illustration, 1 mark for which criterion to follow in each situation, 1 mark for the indivisibility limitation.
official_questions.mistake: Answering only that 'NPV and IRR always agree for a single project' — true, but about a different pair of techniques, and irrelevant when the question is about ranking. The second is asserting that PI is always superior because it is relative: it is superior only when capital is the binding constraint.

mcqs.question: Three projects have discounted cash outflows of ₹5,50,000, ₹75,000 and ₹1,00,20,000 and discounted cash inflows of ₹6,50,000, ₹95,000 and ₹1,00,30,000. Which project has the highest desirability factor?

options.A: The first, because its inflows exceed its outflows by ₹1,00,000
options.B: The third, because it generates the largest cash inflows
options.C: The second, with a factor of 1.27
options.D: All three are equally desirable, since each has a factor above 1

mcqs.explanation: SM Illustration 5: the desirability factors are ₹6,50,000 ÷ ₹5,50,000 = 1.18, ₹95,000 ÷ ₹75,000 = 1.27, and ₹1,00,30,000 ÷ ₹1,00,20,000 = 1.001. ICAI's own comment is that in absolute terms project 3 gives the highest cash inflows yet its desirability factor is low, because the outflow is also very high.

why_wrong.A: ₹1,00,000 of surplus on a ₹5,50,000 outlay is a factor of 1.18 — second, not first.
why_wrong.B: The size of the inflows is exactly what the factor is designed to look past.
why_wrong.D: All three are acceptable, but the factor ranks them and they are not equal.

mcqs.trap: The smallest project wins; that is the whole purpose of a relative measure.

mcqs.question: According to the study material, the profitability index fails as a guide:

options.A: Whenever the cost of capital changes during the project's life
options.B: Whenever a project has more than one internal rate of return
options.C: Whenever the project's cash flows are not uniform
options.D: In resolving capital rationing where projects are indivisible

mcqs.explanation: SM §9.2, limitations of PI: the profitability index fails as a guide in resolving capital rationing where projects are indivisible, and once a single large project with high NPV is selected the possibility of accepting several small projects which together may have a higher NPV is excluded.

why_wrong.A: A changing cost of capital is a difficulty for every discounted technique, and is not the limitation ICAI records for PI.
why_wrong.B: Multiple IRR is a limitation of IRR (§9.3.4).
why_wrong.C: Uneven cash flows make the arithmetic longer but do not impair the ratio.

mcqs.trap: PI is the right tool for capital rationing when projects are divisible, and the wrong one when they are not — §11.1 draws exactly that line.

recap: PI = discounted inflows ÷ discounted outflows; also called the desirability factor or present value index.
Accept if PI ≥ 1; among mutually exclusive projects the higher PI (and under §10, where NPV is the same, the highest PI).
PI = 1 + NPV ÷ I, so PI and NPV never disagree on accept-reject but often disagree on ranking.
PI fails where capital is rationed and projects are indivisible.

concepts.title: 9.3–9.3.1 The Internal Rate of Return Method and its Acceptance Rule
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (May 2025 Q3(a), May 2026 MCQ 7 and MCQ 8) · RTP 0 · MTP 2 (Mar 2024 Series I, May 2025 Series II)
understand: ==The IRR method considers the time value of money, the initial cash investment and all cash flows from the investment — but **unlike NPV it does not use the desired rate of return; it estimates the discount rate that makes the present value of subsequent cash inflows equal to the initial investment**. That discount rate is the IRR.==

==**IRR definition** (SM §9.3): ==**Internal rate of return for an investment proposal is the discount rate that equates the present value of the expected cash inflows with the initial cash outflow.**== The IRR is then compared with a criterion rate of return — the organisation's desired rate for evaluating capital investments.

==**Scenario 1 — uniform cash flows.** Total initial investment = Annual cash inflow × annuity discount factor for the discount rate and the number of periods, so
**A = Total initial cash disbursements and commitments ÷ Annual (equal) cash inflows**.
Once A is calculated, search for it in the **PVAF table** in the row for the project's life. If the exact value of A is found, the corresponding interest rate **is** the IRR; since that rarely happens, follow the steps below.==

==**The four steps when A is not in the table** (SM §9.3): **1.** Compute the approximate payback period, also called the **fake payback period**. **2.** Locate that value in the PVAF table against the project's life; it will fall between two discounting rates. **3.** Discount the cash flows using **both** rates. **4.** Interpolate:
==**IRR = LR + [NPV at LR ÷ (NPV at LR − NPV at HR)] × (HR − LR)**==
or equivalently
==**IRR = LR + [(PV at LR − CI) ÷ (PV at LR − PV at HR)] × (HR − LR)**==
where LR = lower rate, HR = higher rate and CI = capital investment.

**SM Illustration 6, the annuity route.** Outlay ₹10,00,000, annual inflow ₹2,50,000 for 6 years, salvage nil. Fake payback = ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹2,50,000 = **4**. In the 6-year row, 4 lies between 4.111 (12%) and 3.998 (13%). NPV at 12% = +₹27,750; NPV at 13% = −₹500. ==**IRR = 12% + [27,750 ÷ 28,250] × 1% = 12.978%.**==

==**Scenario 2 — non-uniform cash flows.** Discount at any random rate, say 10%, 15% or 20%. If the resulting NPV is **negative**, discount again at a **lower** rate to make it positive; if **positive**, discount again at a **higher** rate to make it negative. Then interpolate with the same formula.==
**SM Illustration 7.** Investment ₹1,36,000 with inflows ₹30,000, ₹40,000, ₹60,000, ₹30,000 and ₹20,000. At 10% the NPV is +₹2,280; at 12% it is −₹4,190. ==**IRR = 10 + [2,280 ÷ 6,470] × 2 = 10.704%.**==

**SM Illustration 8, the one that starts from profit.** Capital cost ₹3,60,000, life 5 years, salvage nil, net operating income after depreciation ₹68,000 a year, tax 45%. ==Cash inflow = ₹68,000 − tax ₹30,600 = PAT ₹37,400 **plus depreciation ₹72,000** = **₹1,09,400**.== PVAF required = ₹3,60,000 ÷ ₹1,09,400 = **3.29**, which falls between 15% (3.35) and 16% (3.27). PV of inflows ₹3,66,490 and ₹3,57,738, giving NPVs of +₹6,490 and −₹2,262. ==**IRR = 15 + [6,490 ÷ 8,752] × 1 = 15.74%.**==

==**Acceptance Rule** (SM §9.3.1). The use of IRR as a criterion involves a comparison of IRR with the required rate of return, known as the ==**cut-off rate**==. **The project should be accepted if IRR is greater than the cut-off rate. If IRR is equal to the cut-off rate the firm is indifferent. If IRR is less than the cut-off rate the project is rejected.** Formally:
==**If IRR ≥ Cut-off Rate or WACC — Accept** the proposal. **If IRR < Cut-off Rate or WACC — Reject** it.==

==**What the cut-off rate is** (MTP Mar 2024 Series I, ICAI's own words): **'It is the minimum rate which the management wishes to have from any project. Usually this is based upon the cost of capital. The management gains only if a project gives return of more than the cut-off rate. Therefore, the cut-off rate can be used as the discount rate or the opportunity cost rate.'**==

==**Advantages of IRR** (SM §9.3): it **makes use of the concept of time value of money**; **all the cash flows in the project are considered**; it is **easier to use, as an instantaneous understanding of desirability can be determined by comparing it with the cost of capital**; and it **helps in achieving the objective of maximisation of shareholders' wealth**.==

==**Limitations of IRR** (SM §9.3): **the calculation process is tedious** if there is more than one cash outflow interspersed between the inflows, and **there can then be multiple IRR, the interpretation of which is difficult**; the approach **creates a peculiar situation if we compare two projects with different inflow/outflow patterns**; **it assumes all future cash inflows are reinvested at a rate equal to the IRR**, ignoring the firm's ability to reinvest at a portfolio of different rates; and **where mutually exclusive projects have considerably different cash outlays, a project with a larger fund commitment but a lower IRR contributes more in terms of absolute NPV and increases shareholders' wealth** — so a decision based only on IRR may not be correct.==

official_questions.question: Data for a capital project: annual interim cash inflows for the first two years ₹1,00,000; annual interim cash inflows for the next two years ₹80,000; useful life 4 years; salvage value at the end of the project ₹50,000; internal rate of return 12%; cost of capital 10%. Calculate (i) initial investment, (ii) net present value, (iii) profitability index, (iv) discounted payback period, (v) MIRR. PVIF at 9%, 10%, 11% and 12% and compounding factors at 10% and 12% are given.
answer_points: ==**(i) Initial investment — the whole question turns on this step.** **Using IRR = 12%, the NPV is zero, so the initial investment equals the present value of the inflows at 12%.** Year 1 ₹1,00,000 × 0.893 = ₹89,300; year 2 ₹1,00,000 × 0.797 = ₹79,700; year 3 ₹80,000 × 0.712 = ₹56,960; year 4 ₹80,000 × 0.636 = ₹50,880; salvage ₹50,000 × 0.636 = ₹31,800. ==**Initial investment = ₹3,08,640.**==

**(iv) Discounted payback period.** Discounted flows at 10%: ₹90,900, ₹82,600, ₹60,080 and ₹88,790 (year 4 including the salvage), with cumulative totals ₹90,900, ₹1,73,500, ₹2,33,580 and ₹3,22,370. ==**Discounted payback = 3 + (₹3,08,640 − ₹2,33,580) ÷ ₹88,790 = 3.845 years, or about 3 years 10 months.**==

==**(v) MIRR.** Compound every inflow forward to year 4 at the 10% reinvestment rate: ₹1,00,000 × 1.331 = ₹1,33,100; ₹1,00,000 × 1.210 = ₹1,21,000; ₹80,000 × 1.100 = ₹88,000; ₹80,000 × 1.000 = ₹80,000; salvage ₹50,000 × 1.000 = ₹50,000. **Terminal value = ₹4,72,100.** Then ₹3,08,640 ÷ ₹4,72,100 = 0.654, which in the year-4 row of the present value table corresponds to about **11.20%**. Alternatively total return = ₹4,72,100 ÷ ₹3,08,640 = 1.5296, and **MIRR = 1.5296^(1/4) − 1 = 11.20%**.==

==**Three cross-checks that confirm the whole answer.** The NPV at 10% is positive because 10% is **below** the IRR of 12% — the two statements are the same statement. The PI of 1.0445 equals 1 + (₹13,730 ÷ ₹3,08,640), as it must. And the MIRR of 11.20% lies **between the cost of capital (10%) and the IRR (12%)**, which is where a MIRR always lies when the reinvestment rate is below the IRR.==

**Why the salvage value is compounded at a factor of 1.000.** It is received **at the end of year 4**, which is the terminal date, so it is reinvested for zero years. The same is true of the year-4 operating inflow — a point SM §9.5 makes explicitly.
official_questions.conclusion: Initial investment ₹3,08,640; NPV ₹13,730; PI 1.0445; discounted payback 3.845 years; MIRR about 11.20%. Five techniques from one chain, all opened by the IRR.

official_questions.question: Details of a project: initial outlay ₹800 lakhs; NPV at a 16% discount rate ₹50.71 lakhs; NPV at a 20% discount rate ₹(26.84) lakhs. What will be the internal rate of return of the project? If the cost of capital is 18.50%, should the project be accepted? (A) 16.00%, Yes (B) 18.62%, Yes (C) 18.00%, Yes (D) 18.62%, No
answer_points: ==**Then apply the acceptance rule** (SM §9.3.1): IRR 18.62% **is greater than** the cut-off rate of 18.50%, so **the project should be accepted**. The answer is **(B) 18.62%, Yes.**==

**Why (D) is the trap.** It carries the right IRR and the wrong decision — set for candidates who interpolate correctly and then compare carelessly. The margin is only 0.12 percentage points, so the comparison has to be made deliberately rather than by eye.
**Why (A) and (C) are wrong.** 16.00% is the lower trial rate, not the IRR; 18.00% is a rounding that the interpolation does not support.

**The initial outlay of ₹800 lakhs is not needed.** Both NPVs are already net of it. ==A figure given in a question is not always a figure the answer uses — and spotting that is part of what a 1-mark MCQ tests.==

**Sanity check without the formula.** The NPV falls from +50.71 to −26.84 across 4 percentage points, so zero is crossed about 50.71/77.55 = 65% of the way along, that is at roughly 16 + 2.6 = 18.6%. The estimate alone eliminates (A) and (C).
official_questions.conclusion: Option (B): IRR 18.62%, and since that exceeds the 18.50% cut-off, accept.

official_questions.question: FG Ltd. is appraising a one-year investment plan which requires an initial outlay of ₹1,00,000 and will mature at ₹1,25,000 at the end of the term. The plan has a beta of 1.3, the risk free rate of return is 10% and the market rate of return is 18%. Calculate the required rate of return and decide whether the plan is worthwhile. (A) 25%, not worthwhile (B) 20.4%, not worthwhile (C) 20.4%, worthwhile (D) 25%, worthwhile
answer_points: ==**Step 1 — the required rate of return from CAPM** (FM Ch 4 §6): Ke = Rf + β (Rm − Rf) = 10% + 1.3 × (18% − 10%) = 10% + 10.4% = ==**20.4%**==. This is the plan's **cut-off rate**, risk-adjusted for its beta.
==**Step 2 — the plan's own return.** A one-year investment of ₹1,00,000 maturing at ₹1,25,000 earns ₹25,000, or **25%**. For a single-period investment that return **is** the IRR.==
==**Step 3 — the acceptance rule** (SM §9.3.1): the return of **25% exceeds the cut-off rate of 20.4%**, so **the plan is worthwhile**. The answer is **(C) 20.4%, worthwhile.**==

**Why the two numbers in each option matter separately.** (A) and (D) use 25% as the required return — confusing the plan's return with the rate it must beat. (B) has the right required return and the wrong verdict.

==**What this MCQ is really testing.** It is the only official question in the chapter where the **cut-off rate has to be computed rather than given**, and it uses CAPM to do it — so Chapter 4's cost of equity and Chapter 7's acceptance rule meet in one two-mark question.==

**Equivalently, by NPV.** PV of ₹1,25,000 at 20.4% = ₹1,25,000 ÷ 1.204 = ₹1,03,820, so the NPV is +₹3,820 — positive, and the same conclusion. Either route is acceptable; the NPV route is the safer one if the arithmetic of a percentage comparison feels uncertain.
official_questions.conclusion: Option (C): required return 20.4% from CAPM, actual return 25%, so the plan is worthwhile.

official_questions.question: WRITE a short note on "Cut-off Rate". (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**ICAI's own answer, worth learning verbatim:** '**It is the minimum rate which the management wishes to have from any project. Usually this is based upon the cost of capital. The management gains only if a project gives return of more than the cut-off rate. Therefore, the cut-off rate can be used as the discount rate or the opportunity cost rate.**'==

**Where it comes from.** SM §9 explains that theoretically the desired rate of return is the return available on the best alternative investment of the same risk; because that is hard to identify, an organisation sets a **minimum rate that all capital projects must meet**, based perhaps on an industry average or the cost of other investment opportunities, and **many organisations use the WACC**.

==**Where it is used.** It is the comparator in the **IRR acceptance rule** (§9.3.1): accept if IRR ≥ cut-off rate, be indifferent if equal, reject if below. It serves equally as the **minimum acceptable rate of return** in the ARR rule of §8.2 and §10 — ICAI's own ARR illustration uses a 20% cut-off below which proposals are automatically rejected.==

**And why it can play three roles at once.** Because the minimum acceptable return, the discount rate and the opportunity cost rate are, in a well-run firm, the same number: the return the funds could earn elsewhere at the same risk.
official_questions.conclusion: The minimum return management requires, usually based on the cost of capital, serving as the discount rate, the opportunity cost rate and the IRR comparator.

official_questions.question: WRITE a short note on internal rate of return. (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Definition.** The internal rate of return for an investment proposal is **the discount rate that equates the present value of the expected cash inflows with the initial cash outflow** — equivalently, the rate at which the project's NPV is zero.==

**How it differs from NPV.** The IRR method considers the time value of money, the initial cash investment and all the cash flows, but **it does not use the desired rate of return**; instead it **estimates** the rate that makes the inflows equal the investment, and that rate is then compared with a criterion rate.

==**How it is computed.** For uniform inflows, the annuity factor A = investment ÷ annual inflow is located in the PVAF table against the project's life. Where it falls between two rates, discount at both and interpolate: **IRR = LR + [NPV at LR ÷ (NPV at LR − NPV at HR)] × (HR − LR)**.==
==**The acceptance rule** (§9.3.1): **accept if IRR ≥ the cut-off rate or WACC; the firm is indifferent if the two are equal; reject if IRR is below it.**==

**Advantages and limitations, in a line each.** It uses the time value of money, considers all cash flows, and gives an immediately comparable percentage. But the calculation is tedious where outflows are interspersed among inflows, **multiple IRRs can then arise**, it **assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself**, and on mutually exclusive projects of different size a lower-IRR project may add more to shareholders' wealth.
official_questions.conclusion: The rate at which NPV is zero, compared against the cut-off rate — powerful, but resting on a reinvestment assumption NPV does not make.

concepts.title: 9.3.2–9.3.4 IRR and Mutually Exclusive Projects, the Reinvestment Assumption, and Multiple IRR
understand: ==**Projects are called mutually exclusive when the selection of one precludes the selection of others** — ICAI's example is a company owning one piece of land that can be used either for project S or for project L.==

==**The crossover rate.** On ICAI's chart, as long as the cost of capital is **greater than the crossover rate of 7%**, NPV(S) is larger than NPV(L) **and** IRR(S) exceeds IRR(L), so both methods choose S. **But if the cost of capital is less than 7%, the NPV method ranks project L higher while the IRR method still indicates S is better.** ==**Mutually exclusive projects can create problems with the IRR technique, because IRR is expressed in percentage and does not take into account the scale of investment or the quantum of money earned.**==

**SM Example 8 — the clearest case in the chapter.** Project A: outflow ₹1,00,000 in year 0, inflow ₹1,50,000 in year 1, **IRR 50%**, **NPV at 10% ₹36,360**. Project B: outflow ₹5,00,000, inflow ₹6,25,000, **IRR 25%**, **NPV at 10% ₹68,180**. ==Project A earns a higher return, but project B's NPV is larger. Accepting A means the total investment is ₹4,00,000 less than it would have been under B, and ==**selection of Project A implies rejection of an opportunity to earn an additional ₹31,820 (₹68,180 − ₹36,360) for the shareholders — a reduction in shareholders' wealth.**==

==Nor is it safe to assume that a choice can be made using IRR even when the **larger** project also has the **higher** IRR.== **SM Example 9.** Project A: outflow ₹9,00,000 with inflows ₹7,00,000, ₹6,00,000, ₹4,00,000 and ₹50,000; Project B: outflow ₹8,00,000 with inflows ₹62,500, ₹6,00,000, ₹6,00,000 and ₹6,00,000. ==**IRR of A = 46%, IRR of B = 35%** — A is both larger and higher-returning. Yet at a discount rate of 5%, **NPV of A = ₹6,97,535 and NPV of B = ₹8,15,625**, so **B should be selected**.== ICAI's explanation: *this type of anomalous situation arises due to the reinvestment assumptions implicit in the two evaluation methods.*

==**9.3.3 The Reinvestment Assumption.** **The NPV technique assumes that all cash flows can be reinvested at the discount rate used for calculating the NPV** — a logical assumption, since using NPV implies that all projects providing a higher return than the discounting factor are accepted. ==**In contrast, the IRR technique assumes that all cash flows are reinvested at the project's IRR.**== This means **projects with heavy cash flows in the early years will be favoured by the IRR method** relative to projects with larger cash flows in later years — which is why Example 9's Project A, whose inflows are front-loaded, is preferred by IRR and rejected by NPV.

==**9.3.4 Multiple Internal Rate of Return.** ==**Where project cash flows change signs or reverse during the life of a project** — for example an initial cash outflow followed by cash inflows and subsequently followed by a major cash outflow — **there may be more than one IRR.**== On ICAI's graph of discount rate against NPV the curve crosses zero twice. ==**If the cost of capital is less than both IRRs a decision can be made easily; otherwise the IRR decision rule may turn out to be misleading, as the project should only be invested in if the cost of capital is between IRR₁ and IRR₂.**== Understanding this requires understanding the implicit reinvestment assumption in both techniques.

**The practical reading of all three sub-sections together.** IRR is a percentage, and a percentage has no size. It cannot tell you how much wealth a project creates, it silently assumes you can reinvest at its own rate, and if the sign of the cash flows reverses it may not even be unique. ==**None of this makes IRR wrong — it makes NPV the tie-breaker.**==

concepts.title: 9.4–9.5 Discounted Payback Period and the Modified Internal Rate of Return
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 (asked inside May 2024 Q3(a), Sep 2024 Part I and May 2025 Q3(a)) · RTP 1 (Sep 2026) · MTP 3 (Jan 2025 Series I, Mar 2024 Series II, May 2025 Series II)
understand: ==**The discounted payback period** (SM §9.4) is the same as the payback period of §8.1 ==**except that the cash flows here are discounted at a predetermined rate**==. Payback period is the time required for cumulative cash inflows to recover the cash outflows of the project. ==**This technique is considered superior to the simple payback period method because it takes into account the time value of money.**==

**SM Example 10, which shows how big the difference can be.** A ₹30,000 outlay with annual inflows of ₹6,000 has a simple payback of **5 years** (₹30,000 ÷ ₹6,000). Discounting the inflows at a 15% required rate gives present values of ₹5,220, ₹4,536, ₹3,948, ₹3,432, ₹2,982, ₹2,592, ₹2,256, ₹1,962, ₹1,704 and ₹1,482, whose cumulative total after ten years is ₹30,114. ==**The discounted payback is therefore approximately 10 years against 5 years under simple payback** — and ICAI's own comment: **as the required rate of return increases, the distortion between simple payback and discounted payback grows.**==

==**Modified Internal Rate of Return** (SM §9.5). MIRR addresses several of IRR's deficiencies: ==**it eliminates multiple IRR rates; it addresses the reinvestment rate issue; and it produces results consistent with the Net Present Value method.**== It is also called the ==**Terminal Value method**==.

==**How MIRR works.** **All cash flows, apart from the initial investment, are brought to the terminal value using an appropriate discount rate — usually the Cost of Capital.** This gives a single stream of cash inflow in the terminal year. ==**The MIRR is obtained by assuming a single outflow in the zeroth year and the terminal cash inflow; the discount rate which equates the present value of the terminal cash inflow to the zero-year outflow is the MIRR.**==
==**Decision criterion.** The same as IRR: **accept an investment if MIRR is larger than the required rate of return, and reject it if MIRR is lower.**==

**SM Illustration 9 worked through.** An investment of ₹1,36,000 yields ₹30,000, ₹40,000, ₹60,000, ₹30,000 and ₹20,000 (profits before depreciation but after tax); cost of capital 8%.

| Year | Cash flow (₹) | Reinvestment factor at 8% | Terminal value (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30,000 | 1.3605 | 40,815 |
| 2 | 40,000 | 1.2597 | 50,388 |
| 3 | 60,000 | 1.1664 | 69,984 |
| 4 | 30,000 | 1.0800 | 32,400 |
| 5 | 20,000 | 1.0000 | 20,000 |
| | | | **2,13,587** |

==The factor for year 1 is 1.08⁴ = 1.3605 because ₹1 at the end of year 1 is reinvested for **four** years to reach the end of year 5; and **the year-5 flow is reinvested for zero years, so its factor is 1**.==

==**Two routes to the answer.** ₹1,36,000 ÷ ₹2,13,587 = **0.6367**, and reading 0.6367 along the year-5 row of the present value table gives a return of **9%**. Or: total return = ₹2,13,587 ÷ ₹1,36,000 = **1.5705**, and **MIRR = 1.5705^(1/5) − 1 = 9%**.==

**The cross-check worth carrying into the exam.** The same cash flows have an **IRR of 10.704%** (SM Illustration 7) and a **MIRR of 9%** at a cost of capital of 8%. ==**MIRR always lies between the cost of capital and the IRR when the reinvestment rate is below the IRR** — so if your MIRR comes out above the IRR or below the cost of capital, the compounding factors are wrong.==

**Why both techniques are examined so often despite being 'extras'.** The discounted payback period is the only technique that answers the question a banker asks — how long until the money is back, in real terms — and MIRR is the only one that repairs IRR's reinvestment assumption. Between them they appeared in three past-paper questions, one RTP and three MTPs in three years.

official_questions.question: P Limited is evaluating two mutually exclusive investment alternatives, Machine I and Machine II. Cost of capital 12%; tax 30%. Machine I: initial cost ₹10,00,000, useful life 5 years, annual income before depreciation and tax ₹3,45,000. Machine II: initial cost ₹15,00,000, useful life 6 years, annual income before depreciation and tax ₹4,55,000. Straight line depreciation over each machine's useful life. Required: (i) compute the discounted payback period, NPV and IRR for each machine; (ii) advise the management. (ICAI label: Capital Budgeting Decision.)
answer_points: **Cash inflows.** Depreciation: Machine I ₹10,00,000 ÷ 5 = **₹2,00,000**; Machine II ₹15,00,000 ÷ 6 = **₹2,50,000**. Income before tax ₹1,45,000 and ₹2,05,000; less tax at 30% ₹43,500 and ₹61,500; income after tax ₹1,01,500 and ₹1,43,500; add depreciation back for ==**annual cash inflows of ₹3,01,500 and ₹3,93,500**==.

==**(ii) The three criteria split two to one.** Discounted payback ranks **Machine I** first; NPV ranks **Machine II** first; IRR ranks **Machine I** first. ICAI's advice: *'Since Machine I has better ranking than Machine II, therefore Machine I should be selected.'*==

==**Two reservations to carry, because ICAI's own reasoning here is not the chapter's own rule.** First, §9.1 and §10 make the **NPV criterion decisive** — it is the measure in conformity with wealth maximisation — and on NPV Machine II wins by ₹31,165. Second, the machines have **unequal lives** (5 years against 6), which is exactly the situation §11.2 says must be handled by the replacement chain or the equivalent annualised criterion rather than by raw comparison. On the equivalent annualised criterion, Machine I gives ₹86,909 ÷ 3.605 = **₹24,108** a year and Machine II ₹1,18,074 ÷ 4.111 = **₹28,721** a year, which points to **Machine II**.==

**How to answer it in the exam.** Reproduce ICAI's computation and its majority-of-rankings advice, then add one sentence noting that on the NPV criterion, and on an equivalent annualised comparison given the unequal lives, Machine II would be preferred. ==That sentence is the difference between repeating an answer and understanding it.==

official_questions.question: EXPLAIN the concept of discounted payback period. (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Definition.** The discounted payback period is **the payback period computed on cash flows that have been discounted at a predetermined rate** — otherwise it is the same technique as the simple payback period of §8.1: **the time required for cumulative cash inflows to recover the cash outflows of the project**.==

==**Why it exists.** The problem with the simple payback period is that **it ignores the time value of money**. Discounting the inflows before cumulating them corrects that, which is why ==**this technique is considered superior to the simple payback period method**==.

**How it is computed.** Discount each year's net cash inflow at the required rate; cumulate the discounted figures; the discounted payback period is the year in which the cumulative total reaches the initial outlay, plus the fraction of the following year, the fraction being the balance of the outlay divided by **that year's discounted inflow**.

==**ICAI's own illustration of the size of the correction.** A ₹30,000 outlay with annual inflows of ₹6,000 has a simple payback of **5 years**. Discounted at 15%, the cumulative discounted inflows reach ₹30,114 only after **ten years** — so the discounted payback is about **10 years**. And ICAI adds: **as the required rate of return increases, the distortion between simple payback and discounted payback grows.**==

**What it still does not do.** Like the simple payback period, it **ignores cash flows arising after the payback point**, so it measures recovery of capital rather than total profitability. It is a liquidity and risk screen, not a wealth measure.
official_questions.conclusion: The payback period computed on discounted cash flows — superior to simple payback because it respects the time value of money, but still blind to everything after recovery.
keywords: ignores the time value of money

official_questions.question: A firm can invest in either of two projects; its cost of capital is 10%. Pre-tax cash flows, year 0 to year 5 — Project A: ₹(2,00,000), ₹35,000, ₹80,000, ₹90,000, ₹75,000, ₹20,000; Project B: ₹(2,00,000), ₹2,18,000, ₹10,000, ₹10,000, ₹4,000, ₹3,000. Ignore taxation. An amount of ₹35,000 will be spent on sales promotion in year 3 for Project A, which has not been taken into account in the pre-tax cash flows. PVF at 10%: 1, 0.91, 0.83, 0.75, 0.68, 0.62. Calculate for each project (i) the discounted payback period, (ii) the desirability factor, (iii) the net present value.
answer_points: ==**First adjust Project A's year-3 flow.** The ₹35,000 of sales promotion has 'not been taken into account', so Project A's year-3 inflow becomes ₹90,000 − ₹35,000 = **₹55,000**. Candidates who miss this one line get every one of the three answers wrong for Project A.==

**(i) Discounted payback period.** ==**Project A:** cumulative discounted inflows reach ₹1,90,500 by the end of year 4, leaving ₹9,500 of the ₹2,00,000 outlay to come out of year 5's discounted inflow of ₹12,400, so **DPP = 4 + (₹9,500 ÷ ₹12,400) = 4.766 years**, or 4 years 9 months and 6 days.==
==**Project B:** year 1's discounted inflow alone is ₹1,98,380, leaving only ₹1,620 to come from year 2's ₹8,300, so **DPP = 1 + (₹1,620 ÷ ₹8,300) = 1.195 years**, or 1 year 2 months and 10 days.==
**(iii) NPV.** ==**Project A ₹2,900; Project B ₹18,760.**==

==**All three criteria agree, for once — and the reason is worth naming.** Project B recovers almost the whole outlay in year 1, so almost none of its value is lost to discounting; Project A spreads its inflows over five years and loses a great deal. **Project B is the textbook front-loaded project**, which is exactly the shape §9.3.3 says the IRR method flatters — and here even NPV agrees, because the two outlays are identical and so scale is not in play.==

**A useful contrast to hold.** Project A's total undiscounted inflow after the promotion adjustment is ₹2,65,000 against Project B's ₹2,45,000 — **A earns more money in total, and B is worth more today.** That one comparison is the clearest demonstration of the time value of money in the whole official question set.
official_questions.conclusion: Project A: DPP 4.766 years, PI 1.01, NPV ₹2,900. Project B: DPP 1.195 years, PI 1.09, NPV ₹18,760. Project B on every criterion.
keywords: sales promotion not taken into account

official_questions.question: DEFINE Modified Internal Rate of Return method. (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Definition.** Under the Modified Internal Rate of Return method, **all cash flows apart from the initial investment are brought to the terminal value using an appropriate discount rate, usually the cost of capital**. This results in a single stream of cash inflow in the terminal year. ==**The MIRR is obtained by assuming a single outflow in the zeroth year and the terminal cash inflow; the discount rate which equates the present value of the terminal cash inflow to the zero-year outflow is the MIRR.**== It is also called the ==**Terminal Value method**==.

==**Why it exists.** Several limitations attach to the conventional IRR, and MIRR addresses them: **it eliminates multiple IRR rates; it addresses the reinvestment rate issue; and it produces results which are consistent with the Net Present Value method.**==
==**Decision criterion.** The same as IRR: **accept the investment if MIRR is larger than the required rate of return, and reject it if MIRR is lower.**==

**The computation in one line.** MIRR = (Terminal value ÷ Initial outflow)^(1/n) − 1, where the terminal value is the sum of each inflow compounded forward at the cost of capital to the end of year n — the final year's inflow carrying a factor of 1.000 because it is reinvested for zero years.

**ICAI's own figures, if an example is wanted.** On an investment of ₹1,36,000 with inflows of ₹30,000, ₹40,000, ₹60,000, ₹30,000 and ₹20,000 at a cost of capital of 8%, the terminal value is ₹2,13,587 and the MIRR is **9%** — against an IRR of 10.704% for the same flows.
official_questions.conclusion: The rate that equates the year-0 outflow to the terminal value of all inflows compounded at the cost of capital — IRR's answer to its own reinvestment assumption.

concepts.title: 9.6–10 NPV against IRR, the Three Scenarios of Conflict, and the Summary of Decision Criteria
understand: ==**What the two methods share** (SM §9.6): **both NPV and IRR are discounted cash flow methods which consider the time value of money**, and **both consider all cash flows over the expected useful life of the investment**.==
==**§9.7 then sets out the three scenarios under which the two methods reach different conclusions.**==

==**Scenario 1 — Scale or Size Disparity.** **Being IRR a relative measure and NPV an absolute measure, in case of disparity in scale or size both may give contradicting ranking.**==
**SM Illustration 10.** Project A: ₹(1,00,000) then ₹50,000, ₹60,000, ₹40,000. Project B: ₹(3,00,000) then ₹1,40,000, ₹1,90,000, ₹1,00,000. Cost of capital 10%.
==**NPV at 10%: A ₹25,050 · B ₹59,300.** **IRR: A 24.26% · B 21.48%.** So NPV prefers B and IRR prefers A — 'thus, there is contradiction in ranking by two methods'.==

==**Scenario 2 — Time Disparity in Cash Flows.** **Overall cash flows may be more or less the same in two projects but there may be a disparity in their timing** — a larger part of the inflows occurring at the beginning in one and at the end in the other.==
**SM Illustration 11.** Project X: ₹(2,50,000) then ₹2,00,000, ₹1,00,000, ₹50,000. Project Y: ₹(3,00,000) then ₹50,000, ₹1,00,000, ₹3,00,000. Cost of capital 10%.
==**NPV at 10%: X ₹51,950 · Y ₹53,350.** **IRR: X 24.87% · Y 17.60%.** NPV prefers Y by a narrow margin; IRR prefers X decisively.==

==**Scenario 3 — Disparity in Life of Proposals (Unequal Lives).** Conflict may arise where two projects, especially mutually exclusive ones, have unequal lives.==
**SM Illustration 12.** Project A: ₹(5,00,000) then ₹7,50,000 and nothing thereafter. Project B: ₹(5,00,000) then ₹2,00,000, ₹2,00,000 and ₹7,00,000. Cost of capital 12%.
==**NPV at 12%: A ₹1,69,750 · B ₹3,36,400.** **IRR: A 50.00% · B 43.07%.** Again a contradiction — and this one is taken further in §11.2.==

==**§10 Summary of Decision Criteria — the single most examinable table in the chapter:**==

| Technique | For an independent project | For mutually exclusive projects |
|---|---|---|
| **Pay Back** (non-discounted) | Payback period **≤** maximum acceptable payback period: **accepted**. Payback period **>** maximum acceptable: **rejected** | Project with the **least** payback period |
| **Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)** (non-discounted) | ARR **≥** minimum acceptable rate of return: **accepted**. ARR **<** minimum: **rejected** | Project with the **maximum** ARR |
| **Net Present Value (NPV)** (discounted) | NPV **≥ 0**: **accepted**. NPV **< 0**: **rejected** | Project with the **highest positive** NPV |
| **Profitability Index (PI)** (discounted) | PI **≥ 1**: **accepted**. PI **< 1**: **rejected** | **When net present value is the same**, the project with the **highest PI** |
| **Internal Rate of Return (IRR)** (discounted) | IRR **≥ K**: **accepted**. IRR **< K**: **rejected** | Project with the **maximum** IRR |

==Two details in that table repay attention. The PI row for mutually exclusive projects is **qualified** — 'when net present value is same' — which is ICAI's own acknowledgement that NPV outranks PI where the two disagree. And the IRR row is **unqualified**, even though §9.3.2 has just spent two illustrations showing that the maximum IRR can be the wrong choice. ==**Where a question makes you choose, choose on NPV, and say why.**==

**How to hold the three scenarios in mind.** They are three ways in which two projects can differ: in **how big** they are, in **when** the money arrives, and in **how long** they last. NPV handles the first and second correctly by construction; it needs the help of §11.2 for the third.

In what situations will they give conflicting results?' The answer separates the two questions — identical on accept-reject, conflicting on ranking whenever the outlays differ.
