concepts.title: 11–11.1 Special Cases: Capital Budgeting under Capital Rationing
understand: ==If a project has a positive NPV it should be accepted, with the objective of maximising shareholders' wealth. But there may be a situation where, **due to resource (capital) constraints — rationing — a firm has to select some projects among various projects, all having positive NPVs.**==

==**Two scenarios decide the method** (SM §11.1):
**(i) Projects are independent of each other and are divisible in nature.** In such a situation ==**the NPV rule should be modified and projects should be ranked on the basis of the 'NPV per rupee of Capital' method.**==
**(ii) Projects are not divisible.** In such a situation ==**projects shall be ranked on the basis of absolute NPV and should be mixed up to the point available resources are exhausted.**==

**SM Illustration 13 — Shiva Limited, worked in full.** Five projects, all with a positive NPV at the company's cut-off rate of 15%, and a capital spending limit of ₹1,20,000:

| Project | Investment (₹'000) | NPV at 15% (₹'000) | NPV per ₹1 invested | Ranking |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | (50) | 15.4 | 0.31 | 5 |
| B | (40) | 18.7 | 0.47 | 2 |
| C | (25) | 10.1 | 0.40 | 3 |
| D | (30) | 11.2 | 0.37 | 4 |
| E | (35) | 19.3 | 0.55 | 1 |

==**The divisible case.** Take the projects in rank order until the ₹1,20,000 is exhausted: E ₹35,000 (NPV ₹19,300), B ₹40,000 (₹18,700), C ₹25,000 (₹10,100), and then **two-thirds of project D** — ₹20,000 of its ₹30,000, giving ₹7,500 of its ₹11,200 NPV. **Total investment ₹1,20,000; total NPV ₹55,600.** ==**Project A is rejected and only two-thirds of project D is undertaken.**==

==**The indivisible case.** Part-projects are now impossible, so combinations must be examined:
**E + B + C** = ₹1,00,000 invested, NPV **₹48,100**
**E + B + D** = ₹1,05,000 invested, NPV **₹49,200**
==**In this case E + B + D would be preferable as it provides a higher NPV despite D ranking lower than C.**==

==**That last sentence is the whole lesson of §11.1, and it is why PI's limitation in §9.2 matters.** A ranking by NPV per rupee is a reliable guide **only when the projects can be sliced**. Once they cannot, the ranking becomes a starting point for examining combinations, and a lower-ranked project can beat a higher-ranked one because it fits the budget better. ==**Rank, then test combinations.**==

**Why both totals fall short of the limit in the indivisible case.** E + B + C spends ₹1,00,000 and E + B + D spends ₹1,05,000, leaving ₹20,000 and ₹15,000 of the ₹1,20,000 unused. Indivisibility means **capital is wasted**, and the best combination is the one that wastes the least value, not the least money.

concepts.title: 11.2 Projects with Unequal Lives
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (May 2026 Q2(a)) · RTP 0 · MTP 1 (Sep 2025 Series I Part I case)
understand: ==**The two problems that raise it** (SM §11.2): **(i) retaining an old asset or replacing it with a new one; (ii) choosing one proposal among two mutually exclusive proposals.** Evaluating these poses no special problem if the proposals have the same life period, **but a problem arises where the projects have unequal lives.**==
==**Two methods** (SM §11.2): **(i) Replacement Chain Method; (ii) Equivalent Annualized Criterion.**==

**SM Illustration 14, which both methods are worked on.** R Pvt. Ltd. is modernising its production facilities and has two proposals. Project A runs six years with cash flows ₹(40,00,000), ₹8,00,000, ₹14,00,000, ₹13,00,000, ₹12,00,000, ₹11,00,000, ₹10,00,000; Project B runs three years with ₹(20,00,000), ₹7,00,000, ₹13,00,000, ₹12,00,000.
==**NPV at 12%: A ₹6,49,094 · B ₹5,15,488. IRR: A 17.47% · B 25.20%.** 'Although from NPV point of view, Project A appears to be better but from IRR point of view, Project B appears to be better. Since both projects have unequal lives, selection on the basis of these two methods shall not be proper.'==

==**(i) Replacement Chain (Common Life) Method.** Since Project A's life is 6 years and Project B's is 3, **to equalise lives we can have a second opportunity of investing in Project B after the first investment runs out**. ==**The NPV of the extended six-year life of Project B is ₹8,82,403, with an IRR of 25.20%** — 'accordingly, with extended life NPV of Project B it appears to be more attractive'.==

==**(ii) Equivalent Annualized Criterion.** The replacement chain **has one drawback: comparing a 3-year project with a 5-year project would require analysing 15 years — the common multiple of the two lives.** The simple solution is the equivalent annualised criterion, in three steps:
==**(a) Compute NPV using the WACC or discounting rate. (b) Compute the Present Value Annuity Factor (PVAF) of that discounting factor for the period of each project. (c) Divide the NPV by the PVAF and compare the values.**==

==**Applied to Illustration 14:**

| | Project A | Project B |
|---|---|---|
| NPV at 12% | ₹6,49,094 | ₹5,15,488 |
| PVAF at 12% | 4.112 (6 years) | 2.402 (3 years) |
| **Equivalent annualised criterion** | **₹1,57,854** | **₹2,14,608** |

==**Thus Project B should be selected** — the project with the lower NPV, because it earns more per year of life.==

==**The formula in one line.** ==**Equivalent annualised NPV = NPV ÷ PVAF for the project's own life at the project's own discount rate.**== Where the NPVs are negative — as they are for two cost-saving warehouses neither of which pays for itself — the same division gives an **equivalent annual cost (EAC)**, and the project with the **least negative** EAC is chosen.

**Why this is the chapter's highest-value single technique for January 2027.** It was asked in a past paper for the first time in May 2026 (7 marks), and in a Part I case in September 2025 Series I (10 marks) a year earlier. It is one short formula, and it **reverses the NPV ranking in both of those official questions** — which is precisely why examiners like it.

**One more cross-reference.** The study material's own **Illustration 18 (HMR Ltd.)** sits in this section as the worked example of problem (i) — retaining an old asset against replacing it — and is the same question as RTP May 2024 FM Q5 with different figures.

official_questions.question: R Ltd. wants to reduce the dependency of manual workforce in its factory by adopting an automatic machine, choosing between Machine M and Machine N, which serve the same job. Purchase cost ₹4,50,000 and ₹3,50,000; estimated useful life 5 years and 7 years; estimated salvage value 10% of cost for each; annual saving in wages ₹11,00,000 and ₹12,00,000; running cost per year excluding depreciation ₹9,00,000 and ₹11,00,000; annual saving in scrap ₹1,00,000 and ₹1,20,000. Cost of capital 9%; tax 25%; SLM depreciation. PVIF and PVIA at 9% are given for years 1 to 7. Required: (i) NPV and profitability index for each machine; (ii) which machine should be selected on the basis of the Equivalent Annualized Criterion?
answer_points: **Annual cash savings.** Total savings (wages + scrap) ₹12,00,000 and ₹13,20,000; less annual running cost ₹9,00,000 and ₹11,00,000; ==**annual cash savings ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,20,000**==. Note that Machine N saves more in wages and scrap but costs far more to run, so on net cash it saves **less**.

**After tax.** Less depreciation gives ₹2,19,000 and ₹1,75,000 before tax; less tax at 25% gives ₹1,64,250 and ₹1,31,250; add depreciation back for ==**annual cash inflows of ₹2,45,250 and ₹1,76,250**==.

==**(ii) Equivalent annualised criterion.** Machine M = ₹5,33,027.25 ÷ 3.889 = **₹1,37,060**. Machine N = ₹5,56,035 ÷ 5.032 = **₹1,10,500**. **So Machine M should be selected on the basis of the Equivalent Annualized Criterion.**==

==**The reversal, stated plainly, because it is the question's whole point.** On NPV, Machine N is better by ₹23,008. On profitability index, Machine N is better, 2.59 against 2.18. **On the equivalent annualised criterion Machine M is better by ₹26,560 a year — and that is the criterion to follow, because the two machines have different lives (5 years and 7).** Machine N's larger NPV is spread over two extra years, which is why it looks better in total and worse per year.==

**Two mechanical points that cost marks.** Each NPV is divided by the PVAF for **its own** life — 3.889 for five years, 5.032 for seven — not by a common factor. And the salvage value is **excluded from the depreciation base and included as a terminal inflow**; counting it in both places, or in neither, changes both answers.

**Part (ii) is only 3 of the 7 marks but it decides the recommendation.** A candidate who computes both NPVs perfectly and then recommends Machine N because its NPV is higher has answered part (i) and contradicted part (ii).
official_questions.conclusion: Machine M: NPV ₹5,33,027.25, PI 2.18, equivalent annualised ₹1,37,060. Machine N: NPV ₹5,56,035, PI 2.59, equivalent annualised ₹1,10,500. Select Machine M.

official_questions.question: Part I case scenario of the September 2025 Series I mock. ABC Ltd., a furniture manufacturer facing delivery delays, will build one of two warehouses. Warehouse Baton: initial cost ₹40,00,000, useful life 5 years, annual net savings before tax ₹12,00,000, ₹14,00,000, ₹10,00,000, ₹10,00,000 and ₹13,00,000, mid-life major maintenance ₹5,00,000 in year 3, salvage value ₹5,00,000 and shutdown and disposal cost ₹1,00,000 in year 5. Warehouse Katon: initial cost ₹60,00,000, useful life 8 years, annual net savings before tax ₹10,00,000 in years 1–2, ₹15,00,000 in years 3–6 and ₹12,00,000 in years 7–8, maintenance ₹2,00,000 in year 4 and ₹3,00,000 in year 7, salvage value ₹8,00,000 and shutdown and disposal cost ₹1,50,000 in year 8. Tax 30%; after-tax cost of capital 10%; SLM depreciation. The five MCQs ask for the NPV of Baton, its EAC, the NPV of Katon, its EAC, and which warehouse should be chosen.
answer_points: ==**Depreciation is computed on cost less the NET salvage.** Baton: salvage ₹5,00,000 less disposal cost ₹1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000, so depreciation = (₹40,00,000 − ₹4,00,000) ÷ 5 = **₹7,20,000**. Katon: ₹8,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹6,50,000, so depreciation = (₹60,00,000 − ₹6,50,000) ÷ 8 = **₹6,68,750**.==

**Baton's table.** Taxable income = savings − maintenance − depreciation; after-tax profit at 70%; cash inflow = after-tax profit + depreciation. ==Year 3 is the one to watch: savings ₹10,00,000 less maintenance ₹5,00,000 less depreciation ₹7,20,000 gives a **taxable loss of ₹2,20,000**, an after-tax figure of ₹(1,54,000) and still a **positive cash inflow of ₹5,66,000**.== Cash inflows: ₹10,56,000, ₹11,96,000, ₹5,66,000, ₹9,16,000, ₹11,26,000, plus ₹4,00,000 of net salvage in year 5. Total present value at 10% = ₹39,46,635.
==**(v) The conclusion.** 'Warehouse Katon should be chosen as it has the lower Equivalent Annual Cost despite having higher upfront cost' — answer **(b)**.==

==**Why both NPVs are negative, and why that does not end the analysis.** Neither warehouse pays for itself out of its own savings at a 10% cost of capital. But the company **has decided to build one** — the question is which, not whether. Where a choice is unavoidable, **the least-cost option is chosen, and with unequal lives the comparison must be on an annual basis**: Katon's ₹(7,810) a year against Baton's ₹(14,077) a year. Comparing the raw NPVs would also have chosen Katon here, but only by accident — the 3-year life difference is doing most of the work.==

**One drafting inconsistency to note.** Option (ii)(b) is printed in the question paper as ₹(14,071) while ICAI's answer computes ₹(14,077); ₹(53,365) ÷ 3.791 = ₹14,077.3. The option is a rounding or typographical slip, and (b) is the intended key either way.
official_questions.conclusion: Baton NPV ₹(53,365), EAC ₹(14,077); Katon NPV ₹(41,667), EAC ₹(7,810). Choose Katon on the lower equivalent annual cost.
